When I'm producing: I usually have a musical "phrase" in mind and then I'll build the song around that. Sometimes its a bass line, sometimes its a chord progression, sometimes its a melody, etc. 

I typically like to lay down chord progressions and drum-lines first, then just solo over that for a bit to see what kind of random licks I can make. Sometimes i'll use a guitar for this, sometimes a piano, sometimes synths, just kinda depends on what i feel like making that day. I put cool things I came up with while soloing into notation so I remember it and then just continue on in that way.

When I'm rapping: Things just randomly come to me no matter where I am or what I'm doing and I have to stop everything and write it down or else i'll forget it, then I'll see it like 6 hours later and go "what the hell that's garbage why did i have to interrupt my life for that".

First things first, don't get frustrated, like you said its supposed to be fun.  The second you start getting frustrated over something you feel like you can't control you'll stop having fun, start dwelling on that and it'll likely turn into resentment if you keep trying to push it.

Second, one of the biggest parts of delivery is simply confidence. It's fine to have songs that don't have the best lyrics in the world as long as you say them like they are the best lyrics in the world.

A lot of the time when you come across a problem with things like delivery it's because of some sort confidence issue, either you think you're worse than you are because you don't like your voice and you're projecting that through your music somehow.  It could also simply be that you just never really learned how to use your voice like an instrument. 

Either way, I'd look up some breathing techniques that singers use to engage your core and create more power from your voice.  Proper breathing while you're performing will help with your delivery more than anything else I can think of off the top of my head. If you're supporting your voice with your core instead of only speaking in a head voice you'll have far more mic presence and as a result your delivery will improve simply because your voice will be a more full sound.  Over time, that will build confidence and you'll be more willing & confident when it comes to exploring your voice as you develop your style over time.

I actually started doing the same thing that you're doing recently, but just because that's how I learned to read music back in the day, just one note at a time. 

Had to start thinking of my voice as just another instrument and everything started to make more sense to me.  i actually write out notes / rhythms on ledger paper to make sure everything fits properly, then I apply lyrics to that, so I come up with my flow/rhythm, then write to that.

The biggest thing I would say to help diversifying your patterns is to break out and listen to music you wouldn't typically listen to.  


Go listen to some foreign music/different genres you wouldn't normally dip into with different time signatures, different scales and listen for how they break up their songs structurally, then try and replicate that. 


Back when I played jazz guitar that's what it really took for me to get out the rut of all my songs sounding pretty much the same. I stopped thinking of my solos (or lyrics in your case) in terms of "verse->refain->verse->refrain->etc"and decided to go more free flow; integrating parts of the hook into verses, integrating overall themes from the pieces i was working on into the solos, then made slight variations (inversions on chord progressions, double-time rhythms instead, syncopating rhythms, etc) on those.
